exercise1.prompt: triple as a lambda that multiplies its argument by three

cases.name: triple is written as a lambda, not with def
cases.describe: triple made from a lambda expression rather than a def statement

hiddenCases.name: works for any number, not only the one listed

exercise1.hint: A lambda is an expression, so it can sit on the right of an equals sign the way a number can. If your solution has the word def in it, it is not the shape this exercise is asking for.

exercise2.prompt: map() with a lambda to square [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

cases.name: the squaring is done by map, not by a loop or a named function
cases.describe: list(map(...)) with a lambda, and no loop or def doing the work instead

exercise2.hint: A loop and a comprehension both produce the right list, and neither is what this exercise is practising. map applies one function to every item for you; the lambda is that function.

questions.prompt: How many expressions can the body of a lambda contain?
questions.explain: A lambda is a single expression, and its value is what the lambda returns. Anything needing statements, a loop or several steps wants a def.

questions.prompt: What does (lambda x: x * 2)(5) evaluate to?
questions.explain: The lambda is a function like any other, so calling it with 5 substitutes 5 for x and hands back the value of the expression.

questions.prompt: When is def the better choice over a lambda?
choices: The logic needs more than one expression
The function will be called from several places and needs a clear name
questions.explain: Lambdas are for short throwaway functions passed to something else. Taking two arguments is fine for a lambda; needing statements, documentation or a name is not.

questions.prompt: Complete the assignment so square holds a one-line function: square = ___ x: x * x
questions.explain: lambda introduces the parameter list, then a colon, then the single expression the function returns.
